title: The Jesus Prayer
hook: Orthodox Christians repeat Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, with the breath

segments.voice: Yesterday, ACTS: adoration, confession, thanksgiving, supplication. Your line was a shape helps.

Paul tells one of his churches, in the King James Bible: "Pray without ceasing." Taken literally, they're a problem: you have a job, dishes, sleep. How could anyone pray all the time? An old Russian book, written down in the 1800s by an unknown author, The Way of a Pilgrim, tells of a wanderer who hears those words read in church and can't let them go. He walks from town to town, asking priests and monks how it's done. Most give him sermons. Finally an old monk gives him something much smaller: one sentence, said over and over, until it begins to say itself.
screen: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.` → `A WANDERER ASKS HOW.` → `ONE SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: The sentence is the Jesus Prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Many add: a sinner. It's a short prayer with very old roots. On the road out of Jericho, a blind beggar named Bartimaeus hears Jesus passing and shouts, in the King James: "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." People tell him to be quiet; he shouts louder. And in Jesus's story of two men praying in the temple, the tax collector can't even look up; he just says, "God be merciful to me a sinner." Put those two cries together: the Jesus Prayer. By the fourth and fifth centuries, monks in the Egyptian desert repeated short prayers like this all day while they worked. Over centuries the practice was treasured especially in the Orthodox churches, in the monasteries of Mount Athos in Greece, and in Russia. It's sometimes called hesychasm, from the Greek for stillness. Many use a prayer rope, a loop of woven knots, one knot for each prayer. Many join it to the breath: breathing in, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God; breathing out, have mercy on me. And mercy here isn't just let me off. In Greek, have mercy on me is eleison me, the same verb sung in the old church cry, Kyrie eleison, Lord have mercy. Its root, eleos, carries compassion, kindness poured out. Western Christians, Catholic, Anglican and Protestant, have taken up the prayer too. The pilgrim says that in time, it started praying in him, even as he walked.
screen: `BARTIMAEUS SHOUTS LOUDER.` · `GOD BE MERCIFUL TO ME.` · `DESERT, ATHOS, RUSSIA.` · `WITH THE BREATH, ON A ROPE.` · then, large: `HAVE MERCY ON ME.`

segments.voice: If you pray, say it ten times, slowly, with your breath, in on Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, out on have mercy on me, counting on your fingers if it helps. Don't rush; when your mind wanders, just come back to the words. If you don't pray, breathe and listen to the words as someone else's prayer, or rest on a single word, like mercy.
Hesychasm: stillness, sought by repeating a short prayer like the Jesus Prayer, a blind man's shout and a tax collector's whisper, said with the breath.
Your line: have mercy on me. Tomorrow, day one hundred, and a shepherd's psalm. See you there.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me', often many times a day, sometimes with a prayer rope and in rhythm with the breath. Many Catholic, Anglican and Protestant Christians use it too.

what it means: a blind man's shout and a tax collector's whisper, joined into one sentence and said with the breath, so prayer can go on all day.
what a scholar hears: rooted in Mark 10:47 and Luke 18:13, practiced by desert monks, and gathered in the Philokalia (1782); the tradition is called hesychasm, from hesychia, stillness.

chat.says: What is the Jesus Prayer, and how could anyone pray it all day?
options: One line, 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me', repeated, often with the breath.
A long prayer read from a book once each morning, then put away for the day.
A silent method with no words at all, just emptying the mind completely.
chat.meaning: The Jesus Prayer joins Bartimaeus's cry and the tax collector's: one sentence said over and over, often with a prayer rope or the breath.

The Way of a Pilgrim: anonymous, usually dated to the 1850s–1880s; stated as 'written down in the 1800s by an unknown author'.
Desert origins (4th–5th centuries) of repeated short prayers; the fixed wording developed later. Confirm phrasing.
Eleos glossed as compassion and kindness poured out; confirm.
